title: Reading Daniel 2

objectives.can: Read the court scene of Daniel 2 with help only where asked.

explanation.summary: Daniel 2:4 is where the Aramaic of the book begins: the Chaldean wise men speak to the king, and from here to the end of chapter 7 the book is written in Aramaic. The first ten verses are a quarrel between a king and his advisers, told with a handful of patterns you already know: 'answered and said', 'if … then', and דִּי in several jobs.

sections.heading: Where the Aramaic begins
body: The book of Daniel is in two languages. Its first part (to the middle of 2:4) is Hebrew, and the last chapters (8–12) are Hebrew again. The Aramaic runs from 2:4 to the end of chapter 7. The library keeps the two languages as separate editions, so the Aramaic edition opens at 2:4 with the words the Chaldeans say to the king, and your reading starts there.

Why the language changes at this point is a question scholars answer in different ways, and the grammar cannot settle it. For reading, it is enough to notice that the change comes exactly where the wise men begin to speak to the king, and that the Aramaic then goes on through the court stories and the vision of chapter 7.

sections.heading: Court speech and the pattern 'answered and said'
body: The Chaldeans open with a greeting, מַלְכָּא לְעָלְמִין חֱיִי: 'O king, live for ever'. חֱיִי is a Peal imperative, second person masculine singular, and the king is addressed by the determined noun מַלְכָּא. Then comes a polite offer in two clauses: אֱמַר חֶלְמָא, 'tell the dream', also an imperative, and וּפִשְׁרָא נְחַוֵּא, 'and the interpretation we will declare'. The second verb is Pael imperfect, first person plural.

Speakers are introduced by a fixed formula. In 2:5 and 2:8 it is עָנֵה מַלְכָּא וְאָמַר, 'the king answered and said': two Peal participles, masculine singular, joined by וְ, used as a narrative verb. In 2:7 and 2:10 the answer of the Chaldeans is עֲנוֹ … וְאָמְרִין, a perfect (third person plural) followed by a plural participle. The participle says what was done, and the perfect or participle together carry the story on. Read the formula as 'X answered and said' and look for the speech that follows.

sections.heading: 'If … ', the king's threat and the offer
body: The king speaks in conditions. In 2:5 הֵן לָא תְהוֹדְעוּנַּנִי חֶלְמָא וּפִשְׁרֵהּ, 'if you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation', then the punishment follows: הַדָּמִין תִּתְעַבְדוּן, 'you will be made limbs', which means 'cut in pieces', and וּבָתֵּיכוֹן נְוָלִי יִתְּשָׂמוּן, 'and your houses will be made a refuse-heap'. Both verbs are Hithpeel imperfect, a passive-reflexive stem, and the second is plural because its subject is וּבָתֵּיכוֹן, 'and your houses'. The exact sense of נְוָלִי is not certain; lexica give 'refuse-heap' or similar.

In 2:6 the same conditional opens the other side: וְהֵן חֶלְמָא וּפִשְׁרֵהּ תְּהַחֲוֺן, 'but if you declare the dream and its interpretation', and the rewards are given in a list: מַתְּנָן וּנְבִזְבָּה וִיקָר שַׂגִּיא. The imperfect is Haphel, second person masculine plural. The word לָהֵן then restarts the demand: 'therefore (tell me) the dream'. The suffixes -נִי on תְהוֹדְעוּנַּנִי and הַחֲוֺנִי are 'me'. Look for them when a verb seems to have no object.

sections.heading: דִּי in the king's reply and the wise men's answer
body: The two speeches are full of דִּי. In 2:8 the king says יָדַע אֲנָה דִּי עִדָּנָא אַנְתּוּן זָבְנִין, 'I know that you are gaining time': here דִּי introduces what is known ('that'). Next comes כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי חֲזֵיתוֹן, 'inasmuch as you have seen', a three-word group that opens a reason clause. In 2:9 and 2:25 you meet it again as a relative or a conjunction.

In 2:10 the wise men answer that there is no man on earth who can do this: לָא אִיתַי אֲנָשׁ עַל יַבֶּשְׁתָּא דִּי מִלַּת מַלְכָּא יוּכַל לְהַחֲוָיָה. Here אִיתַי is 'there is' and לָא negates it; דִּי is a relative, 'who'; the verb is Peal imperfect, 'can', with a Haphel infinitive after it. The reason follows after כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי: no great and powerful king (כָּל מֶלֶךְ רַב וְשַׁלִּיט) has asked such a thing, with לָא before the verb. A כָּל before a noun with a negative later in the clause is 'no': 'no king has asked'. And in 2:11 מִלְּתָא דִי מַלְכָּה שָׁאֵל יַקִּירָה, 'the thing which the king asks is hard', the relative דִּי introduces a clause with a participle. The word יַקִּירָה has the lexical sense 'honourable', and in this verse it is read as 'difficult' or 'rare'. In the same verse the determined noun is spelled מַלְכָּה, with ה for the ending; the library analyses it as determined all the same.

sections.heading: The decree and the wise men
body: The wise men conclude that only the gods could do it: לָהֵן אֱלָהִין דִּי מְדָרְהוֹן עִם בִּשְׂרָא לָא אִיתוֹהִי. Here לָהֵן is 'except' (after a negative; in 2:6 and 2:9 the same word is read as 'therefore'), and אִיתוֹהִי is אִיתַי with a suffix: 'they are not' (literally 'there is not of them').

The king's anger comes in 2:12: כָּל קֳבֵל דְּנָה, 'for this reason', then two perfects, בְּנַס וּקְצַף, 'was angry and wroth'. He orders the destruction with a Haphel infinitive, לְהוֹבָדָה, 'to destroy'. In 2:13 the decree is carried out: דָתָא נֶפְקַת, 'the decree went out', a Peal perfect, feminine singular, and וְחַכִּימַיָּא מִתְקַטְּלִין, 'and the wise men were being killed'. The participle is Hithpaal, a passive-reflexive stem. Translations differ between 'were being killed' and 'were to be killed'; the form is a participle and the verse leaves the sense open.

sections.heading: Vocabulary of the court
body: The scene has its own words: those for the courtiers, for the thing asked, and for the reward. Learn them together:

head: Word
Plain sense
Where
rows: Chaldeans (here, a class of wise men)

misunderstandings: Reading דִּי as the single word 'of' every time. In this passage it means 'that', 'who' or 'which', and in כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי it belongs to a longer phrase for 'because'. Look at what follows it.
Taking עָנֵה as 'he answers' with a present sense. In 2:5 and 2:8 it is a participle used as the usual narrative formula, 'answered', together with וְאָמַר.
Treating the Hithpeel and Hithpaal verbs as active. תִּתְעַבְדוּן, יִתְּשָׂמוּן and מִתְקַטְּלִין have the prefix of a passive-reflexive stem; the people named are the ones who suffer the action.
Believing that the whole book of Daniel is in Aramaic. Only 2:4 to 7:28 is.

deeper.heading: אַזְדָּא in 2:5 and 2:8
body: The phrase מִלְּתָא מִנִּי אַזְדָּא is read in two main ways. Some take אַזְדָּא as a word of Persian origin meaning 'certain, decided', which gives 'the matter is settled by me'. Others take it as an Aramaic word meaning 'gone', which gives 'the matter has gone from me'. The library glosses it 'sure; assured'. Both readings agree that the king has made up his mind, and the question is disputed.

segments.english: that, if ye make not known unto me the dream, there is but one law for you; and ye have agreed together to speak before me lying and corrupt words, till the time be changed; only tell me the dream, and I shall know that ye can declare unto me the interpretation thereof.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said: 'There is not a man upon the earth that can declare the king's matter; forasmuch as no great and powerful king hath asked such a thing of any magician, or enchanter, or Chaldean.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: And it is a hard thing that the king asketh, and there is none other that can declare it before the king, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: For this cause the king was angry and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise men of Babylon.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: So the decree went forth, and the wise men were to be slain; and they sought Daniel and his companions to be slain.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)
